curriculum.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Solve quadratic equations of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 by factorization, including splitting the middle term
Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a)
Determine the nature of roots using the discriminant b^2 - 4ac
Relate the roots of a quadratic equation to the x-intercepts of its graph
Verify candidate solutions by substituting them back into the original equation
key_concepts: Standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a != 0
The discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines whether roots are real, equal, or complex
Sum and product of roots relationships
Roots of the equation correspond to the x-intercepts of its parabola

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Solve linear equations in one variable
Solve linear inequalities and represent their solutions on a number line
Translate word problems into linear equations and solve them
Verify solutions by substituting them back into the original equation
prerequisites: Arithmetic operations with integers and rational numbers
Collecting like terms and basic algebraic manipulation
key_concepts: A linear equation has degree 1 and at most one solution
Balance property: applying the same operation to both sides preserves equality
The direction of an inequality flips when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Representing solution sets on a number line

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Factorize algebraic expressions by taking out the highest common factor (HCF)
Factorize quadratic expressions by splitting the middle term
Use identities such as a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b) to factorize expressions
Factorize expressions by grouping terms
prerequisites: Algebraic identities: square of a sum, square of a difference, difference of squares
key_concepts: HCF factorization
Splitting the middle term of a quadratic expression
Difference of squares a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)
Perfect square trinomials a^2 ± 2ab + b^2
Factorization by grouping

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Plot points on the Cartesian plane and identify the quadrant of a point
Calculate the distance between two points using the distance formula
Find the midpoint of a line segment using the midpoint formula
Calculate and interpret the slope (gradient) of a line
prerequisites: Cartesian plane basics: axes, ordered pairs, quadrants
key_concepts: Distance formula: sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)
Midpoint formula: ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)
Gradient m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
Signs of coordinates in the four quadrants

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Define the trigonometric ratios sine, cosine, and tangent for a right triangle
Recall and use the trigonometric ratios of special angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
Prove and apply the fundamental identity sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1
Solve right triangles using trigonometric ratios
Solve real-life problems involving angles of elevation and depression
prerequisites: Right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem
key_concepts: SOH-CAH-TOA definitions of the ratios
Special-angle values of sine, cosine, and tangent
Fundamental identity sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1
Angles of elevation and depression

curriculum.subject: Physics
learning_objectives: State Newton's three laws of motion and identify them in everyday situations
Apply F = ma to solve numerical problems
Distinguish between mass and weight, using w = mg
Draw and interpret free-body diagrams
Solve problems using consistent SI units
key_concepts: First law (inertia): with no net force, an object's motion does not change
Second law: net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma)
Third law: action-reaction pairs act on different bodies
Mass (kg) versus weight (N), where weight = mg
Free-body diagrams and net force

curriculum.subject: Physics
learning_objectives: Calculate work done by a constant force using W = F·d·cos θ
Calculate kinetic energy (KE = ½mv^2) and gravitational potential energy (PE = mgh)
State and apply the work-energy theorem
Apply conservation of energy to mechanical problems
Calculate power as the rate of doing work (P = W/t)
prerequisites: Basic vector concepts and force direction
key_concepts: Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force, measured in joules
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv^2
Gravitational potential energy PE = mgh
Work-energy theorem: net work equals the change in kinetic energy
Conservation of mechanical energy
Power = work per unit time, measured in watts

curriculum.subject: Physics
learning_objectives: Describe uniform circular motion and identify centripetal acceleration
Relate linear speed, radius, and time period using v = 2πr/T
Apply the centripetal force relation F = mv^2/r
Explain everyday examples of centripetal force (vehicles on curves, satellites in orbit)
key_concepts: Centripetal acceleration a = v^2/r, always directed toward the center
Centripetal force F = mv^2/r
Relation between linear speed and time period: v = 2πr/T
What supplies the centripetal force: tension, friction, or gravity depending on the situation
